description: We are a team of university students passionate about space exploration and health tech. We joined the NASA Space Apps Challenge to explore innovative ways to monitor and support astronaut health during long-duration space missions. We are currently brainstorming our approach and looking forward to building a great solution!
summary:
AstroKatu is an on-board behavioral health monitor for astronauts on long-duration missions. On a Mars transit, a signal takes up to 22 minutes each way, so a conversation with Earth has a 44-minute round trip. Support that depends on live calls with specialists stops working exactly when a crew member needs it most.

AstroKatu runs on the spacecraft and needs no link to Earth. Each day it gathers sleep and fatigue signals, a reaction-time test, and a three-question check-in led by Katu, a small companion character. It compares every value with the crew member's own adaptive baseline and flags only trends that last several days. Diary text is processed on the device and destroyed, so only structured features are kept. Alerts carry their evidence to a flight surgeon, and nothing acts automatically.

We tested the same personal-baseline logic on real NASA data: blood panels of the Inspiration4 crew from the Open Science Data Repository (OSD-575).
details:
WHAT IT DOES

AstroKatu is an on-board behavioral health monitor for long-duration missions. It gathers health indicators every day, compares them with each crew member's own baseline, and helps the astronaut and the flight surgeon act on sustained changes.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Collect: wearable sleep and vital signs, a reaction-time tap test, and a three-question check-in led by Katu, a companion character.

2. Extract on device: a local language model (Gemma 3 1B through Ollama) turns the diary into a few structured features. The text is destroyed and never leaves the device.

3. Compare: an adaptive individual baseline scores each value against that person's normal range. It freezes while an alert is open and ignores high-workload days, so a decline never becomes the new normal.

4. Apply rules: readable YAML rules look for trends that last several days. A single bad night never raises an alert.

5. Human decides: alerts carry their evidence to a flight surgeon queue. Suggested actions come from a curated library, and nothing is executed automatically.

WHAT WE BUILT

- An interactive web prototype: companion check-in, privacy receipt, personal trends, alert rules, flight surgeon review queue and audit log.

- A FastAPI backend with the baseline, rules engine, action library, scenario simulator and tests.

- A data pipeline that simulates a 180-day mission with 7 crew members and hidden problems, then checks whether the detector finds them.

- An analysis of real NASA data: the pipeline downloads the Inspiration4 crew blood panels from NASA OSDR (study OSD-575) and compares each crew member's post-flight values with their own pre-flight baseline.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

AstroKatu keeps working with no link to Earth, gives the crew member early and private feedback, and gives clinicians explainable evidence instead of a black-box score. It supports decisions and does not diagnose.

TOOLS

Python, pandas, NumPy, FastAPI, SQLite, YAML rules engine, pytest, Ollama with Gemma 3 1B, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Figma, Miro.

CREATIVITY AND WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We replaced the clinical form with a companion the astronaut wants to talk to, and treated privacy as the condition for honest answers. We also considered alert fatigue, false positives from one-off bad days, and the limits of a hackathon prototype: the daily mission data is synthetic and the rules still need clinical validation.
